intro: The long-horizon picture is still dominated by one thing: the AI capex build-out and who captures the economics of it — chips, the hyperscalers funding it, the memory and power feeding it. These are multi-quarter to multi-year theses for perspective, not sized recommendations. The discipline at this horizon is paying a fair price for a durable franchise and sitting still; the levels matter far less than whether the secular story is intact.

ideas.name: NVIDIA
ideas.idea: Own the toll road on AI compute, accumulate on drawdowns.
ideas.why: NVIDIA still sits at the center of the largest capital-spending cycle in tech history, with a CUDA software moat that keeps switching costs high even as competitors ship silicon. At a multi-year horizon the debate isn't whether demand exists, it's the price you pay and margin durability. The structural way to own it is to accumulate on the inevitable 20-30% drawdowns rather than chase strength.
ideas.driver: Hyperscaler + sovereign AI capex compounding for several more years; inference demand following training.
ideas.risk: Custom ASICs (hyperscaler in-house chips) eroding share, or an AI-capex digestion cycle compressing both growth and the multiple at once.

ideas.name: SK Hynix (000660.KS)
ideas.idea: The memory leg of the AI trade, in a tightening oligopoly.
ideas.why: HBM is the supply-constrained input to every accelerator, and the memory industry has consolidated to three players with more pricing discipline than the boom-bust past. As long as accelerator volume grows, HBM content per system grows with it. The cyclicality is real, but the structural setup is the best memory has seen in a decade.
ideas.driver: HBM4 transition and rising HBM content per GPU; disciplined supply from a three-player oligopoly.
ideas.risk: Memory is still cyclical — a demand air-pocket or a capacity race would hit pricing fast.

ideas.name: Microsoft
ideas.idea: The lowest-drama way to own enterprise AI monetization.
ideas.why: Microsoft monetizes AI through Azure, Copilot, and the enterprise software stack it already owns — a diversified, recurring-revenue base that doesn't depend on any single product working. It's the compounder you can hold through cycles while the AI capex story sorts out winners and losers elsewhere. Quality at a fair price, not a cheap stock.
ideas.driver: Azure AI workloads + Copilot attach across the installed base of enterprise seats.
ideas.risk: AI capex outrunning monetization for longer than expected, pressuring free cash flow and the premium multiple.

ideas.name: Alphabet
ideas.idea: Owns the full AI stack and trades at the cohort's lowest multiple.
ideas.why: Alphabet has its own frontier models, custom TPUs, a cloud business inflecting, and search cash flows funding all of it — yet it carries the cheapest valuation among the megacaps because the market fears AI disrupting search. If that disruption proves manageable, the re-rating is the opportunity; the vertical integration is underappreciated.
ideas.driver: TPU-driven cost advantage in inference + Gemini integration across a billion-user surface area.
ideas.risk: Genuine query erosion to AI assistants, or antitrust remedies that fracture the bundle.

ideas.name: SpaceX
ideas.idea: A generational franchise — but let the post-IPO price find reality first.
ideas.why: SpaceX owns launch economics (reusability no one else has matched) and a recurring Starlink subscriber base that is the real long-term value driver. The franchise quality is rare. The problem is purely price: a just-IPO'd, thin-float, hype-priced stock can stay overvalued for a long time. The structural move is to build a position patiently into volatility, not at the IPO peak.
ideas.driver: Starlink subscriber and ARPU growth turning a launch company into a recurring-revenue connectivity utility; Starship lowering cost-to-orbit.
ideas.risk: IPO-cycle overvaluation, key-person concentration, and capital intensity if Starship timelines slip.

ideas.name: Bitcoin
ideas.idea: Hold a small, sized position as a non-correlated store-of-value bet.
ideas.why: At a multi-year horizon Bitcoin's thesis is adoption as a fixed-supply store of value, now with ETF access and growing institutional/treasury ownership broadening the buyer base. It is volatile and not a sure thing, so it belongs as a small, deliberately-sized sleeve you can hold through 50%+ drawdowns — position sizing is the entire risk-management story here.
ideas.driver: Fixed supply meeting widening institutional access (ETFs, treasuries) across halving cycles.
ideas.risk: Regulatory clampdown, a liquidity-crisis drawdown, or the store-of-value narrative simply failing to compound.

ideas.name: Ethereum
ideas.idea: The settlement-layer bet — higher reward, higher uncertainty than BTC.
ideas.why: Ethereum is a bet on programmable settlement and tokenized assets running on its rails, with staking yield and fee burn as value accrual. The upside if on-chain finance scales is larger than Bitcoin's; so is the execution and competitive risk from rival layer-1s. A smaller satellite position to a core BTC holding, for those who want the higher-beta crypto thesis.
ideas.driver: Tokenization of real-world assets + layer-2 scaling driving fee demand and ETH burn.
ideas.risk: Layer-1 competition, regulatory treatment of staking, and slower-than-hoped real-world-asset adoption.
